analysis.one_liner: Caps total interest and fees on consumer loans at 36% a year, with criminal penalties.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Durbin with 4 Democratic cosponsors, the 36% national rate cap was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was filed and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any lender to charge a consumer more than 36% a year once all interest and fees are counted — covering payday loans, car title loans, overdraft fees, and credit cards. It would void loans made above that cap, require lenders to return what borrowers paid, add criminal penalties of prison time and large fines, and let state attorneys general enforce the law. It would also replace the standard APR disclosure on statements with an all-in "FAIR" rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently pay triple-digit rates: the bill's findings say consumers pay about $23.7 billion a year in high-cost overdraft loans and up to $8.1 billion for payday loans, with average annual rates of 400% for payday loans, 300% for car title loans, and up to 3,500% for bank overdraft loans. Under the bill, loans above 36% would be unenforceable and lenders would have to refund everything collected, so borrowers could keep the money at legal cost. State attorneys general and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would gain enforcement tools.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a single national 36% ceiling on the all-in cost of consumer credit — interest, late fees, overdraft fees, credit insurance, and add-on products all count toward it — closing the loopholes, state safe harbors, and rate-exportation tricks that let high-cost lending persist in all 50 states.

Per the bill's own findings, cash-strapped consumers pay on average 400% annual interest on payday loans, 300% on car title loans, and up to 3,500% on bank overdraft loans — roughly $23.7 billion a year on high-cost overdraft loans and up to $8.1 billion on storefront and online payday loans. The 2006 federal 36% cap for servicemembers already 'curbed payday, car title, and tax refund lending around military bases,' which the bill cites as its model.

Gives teeth to the cap: any loan above 36% is null and void, the lender must return all principal, interest, and fees, the borrower can raise the violation as a defense at any time, violations carry up to 1 year in prison and a fine of the greater of three times the debt or $50,000, and state attorneys general can sue to enforce it.

Replaces the APR line on monthly statements with a 'FAIR' rate showing the true all-in fee-and-interest rate, so borrowers can see the real cost of the loan instead of a headline rate that hides fees.
Blocks regulators from granting exemptions to the cap and preserves stricter state rate caps, so the ceiling cannot be quietly lowered or overridden.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and high-cost online installment lenders would lose their core business, and banks and credit card issuers would lose overdraft and high-rate fee income — tens of billions of dollars a year by the bill's own accounting. A smaller cost falls on the highest-risk borrowers, who might find fewer lenders willing to serve them at 36% and could lose access to small-dollar credit altogether rather than pay less for it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and banks collecting fee income

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% all-in cap can make small-dollar lending to high-risk borrowers unprofitable, so some consumers who today use payday or overdraft credit could lose legal access to emergency cash entirely — the same servicemember cap the bill cites as its model 'curbed' those loan products around military bases rather than replacing them with cheaper ones, and the bill's findings concede that affordable alternatives 'should be encouraged' but the bill only encourages, not funds, them.

The enforcement design is unusually harsh: lenders face 1 year in prison and fines of the greater of three times the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation, and every above-cap payment is void with all money returned — a criminal-penalty-plus-total-refund scheme that goes well beyond typical consumer credit rules and could chill mainstream lenders from serving subprime customers at all.

The bill expressly forbids the consumer regulator from granting any exemptions, so there is no flexibility for unusual situations — a rigid cap that cannot be adjusted even if it produces unintended consequences.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large: tens of billions of dollars a year now flowing from cash-strapped households to payday, title, and overdraft lenders would be capped, and the servicemember precedent shows a 36% cap can shut those products down. The honest cost is that a rigid cap with criminal penalties and no exemption authority could leave the riskiest borrowers with no lawful lender at all, and the bill offers no funded alternative for them. A better-designed version would pair the cap with a public or nonprofit small-dollar option; as written, the tradeoff is genuine but falls on a narrow group of borrowers, while the savings flow to millions who pay overdraft and high-rate fees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: On April 9, 2013, Senator Durbin introduced the bill with Senators Blumenthal, Boxer, Merkley, and Whitehouse, making the case that a national 36% cap was needed to close state loopholes and stop triple-digit-rate lending.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the standard first step that sends a bill to the panel with jurisdiction over it.

That was the last action of any kind. The Banking Committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and no version passed either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
Bills that die in committee expire automatically; nothing carried over, and no successor national usury cap became law in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders, along with banks and card issuers collecting overdraft and high-rate fee income — roughly $30 billion a year of charges by the bill's own findings — kept their business models intact because the bill never advanced. Households paying 400% payday rates and up to 3,500% overdraft rates kept paying them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders and banks charging overdraft fees

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks arguing for a national 36% usury cap.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal, Barbara Boxer, Jeff Merkley, and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senators (D-CT, D-CA, D-OR, D-RI), cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction — its entire declared support in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee (Chair Tim Johnson, D-SD)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 9, 2013 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Payday and consumer lending industry
against.what_they_did: Fought national 36% rate caps as a threat to their core product, as they had against similar proposals.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and none was a Republican, but the bill never came to a vote, so the chamber's actual partisan split was never measured.

industries.note: Their business model — average 400% annual rates on payday loans and 300% on car title loans, up to $8.1 billion a year — would be illegal above 36%, with violators' loans void and lenders required to return all collections. The bill cites the servicemember lending cap as proof this model can be shut down.

Overdraft fees — about $23.7 billion a year, at effective rates up to 3,500% — plus late, over-limit, and annual fees all count toward the 36% cap, hitting a major fee-income stream for banks and high-rate card lending. Their interest ran against the borrowers the bill protects.
Online installment lending at triple-digit rates, which the bill's findings flag as an unreported growth area, would fall under the same all-in 36% ceiling with no carve-out.
